question: Before sending anything, an attacker researches a company's CEO using LinkedIn and the company website. Why does this matter?

options.text: It doesn't matter, research isn't hacking
It lets the attacker build a highly convincing, personalized impersonation using entirely public information
It's illegal and rarely actually done
Only very large companies get targeted this way

explanation: None of this requires hacking anything — publicly posted information (who the CEO is, when they're traveling, who handles payments) is enough to make an impersonation attempt convincing.

question: An email from "the CEO" arrives from a domain that's one word different from the real company domain. What should happen?

options.text: It should be trusted, since it looks right at a glance
It should be treated as a major red flag — legitimate email comes from the real domain, not a similar one
It doesn't matter, domains aren't really checked
Reply to confirm, using the same email thread

explanation: A domain that's close but not identical is one of the clearest signs of impersonation — it's designed to read fine at a glance, especially on a phone where the full address often isn't shown.

question: A request combines "please keep this between us" with "I need it within the hour." What does that combination usually signal?

options.text: A legitimate, time-sensitive emergency
It's designed to prevent anyone from having time to verify the request through normal channels
Standard business practice for large transactions
A routine compliance requirement

explanation: Real business decisions this size are rarely both secret and urgent at the same time — that specific combination exists almost entirely to remove the time needed to double-check.

question: What's the safest way to verify an unusual wire transfer request that appears to be from a CEO?

options.text: Reply to the email asking for confirmation
Call the person on a number you already have on file, not one provided in the email
Trust it, since it came from their email address
Ask a coworker if they received the same email

explanation: Verifying through a separate, already-known channel sidesteps the email entirely — replying to the email itself just confirms the request with the same person (or attacker) who sent it.

question: Why is business email compromise so financially damaging compared to many other scams?

options.text: It always targets the largest companies specifically
A wire transfer is typically unrecoverable once it clears, and the amounts involved can be very large
It requires expensive technical tools to pull off
Insurance never covers any part of it

explanation: Unlike a disputed credit card charge, a completed wire transfer usually has no reversal process — a single successful email can result in tens of thousands of dollars with no way to get it back.
